jdw64 · Nov 28, 2026

I can’t laugh at this simulator. When I actually hand things over to AI, it spits out formulas I can’t understand at all. It produces plausible-looking formulas and jargon, and looking at this simulator now, it looks like advanced physics equations, but in reality it has no physical dimensions or conditions of validity. In the past, I tried automating something to see whether AI could do this, and my AI got all excited and sent it to a famous MIT professor from my email (an embarrassing past of mine).The professor was probably baffled too, since he suddenly got an email from some weird lunatic. Since then, I’ve tended to avoid doing things with AI without verifying them myself. Looking at what this simulator is satirizing for example, using approximations without error analysis—it’s nonsense, but the real problem is that there are things that deceive people more cunningly than this satire does. That said, I don’t think at all that AI can’t make discoveries. It’s actually producing results, and I often witness cases where it produces far better results than I do in fields I know well… I don’t know these days. When satire accurately describes reality, it doesn’t seem to be merely funny.

Routine8502 · Nov 28, 2026

LLMs are absolutely helpful in physics research, but the idea that they can solve real problems unattended is, at present, unsupported. I will admit that my applied math skills are relatively weak, so I've been using 6.2 Astra to formalize a numerical physics problem I'm interested in. My god does it go off on all kinds of bizarre tangents, find "solutions" that are totally irrelevant to the problem at hand, and on several occasions basically assume the outcome and proudly tell me that it's found the solution. I've had to spend considerable time reigning it in and directing it towards the relevant problem.

That said, it would have probably taken me 3-4 months to build the background I need to solve this problem, and I'm not sure I would have done it since I wasn't sure the approach would work! And it looks like it's finally converging on the answer.

So I think where the current batch of LLMs are useful for physicists is to prototype solutions to problems where we could solve it, but don't have the time/resources/confidence that there will be an ROI.

Also, I mean, I would never have done a formal asymptotic error analysis. I would have just eyeballed it and gone "eh, good enough". But now I can go make dinner and ask GPT to hammer away at Lean! So I'm pretty satisfied.
